Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Critics say bond financing isn’t the way to do it. For years, California has grappled with a problem that has affected nearly every aspect of our society: The state doesn’t have enough homes that people can afford to live in. Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) aims to address that crisis. It’s estimated that more than 180,000 Californians (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/05/point-in-time-homelessness-report/) are homeless. Rents are so high that a minimum wage worker would need to work 102 hours a week (https://nlihc.org/oor/state/ca) to afford a typical one-bedroom apartment, according to the National Low Income Housing Coalition. A big piece of that problem is construction: Not enough homes are being built. Fewer than a third (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/08/california-rhna-housing-affordable-progress/) of California cities and counties are on track to permit enough market-rate housing to hit their state-mandated targets, and fewer than 6% are on track for very low-income housing. Those targets are based on the state’s assumption that we need nearly 2.5 million more homes. Legislators have passed multiple laws (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/10/newsom-signs-massive-california-housing-overhaul/) trying to address that (https://calmatters.org/education/2026/10/new-laws-affordable-student-housing-california/) by making it easier, faster and cheaper to get projects permitted (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/06/ceqa-urban-development-infill-budget/) and built. Prop. 1 is supposed to supply the money. A recent report estimated (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/03/affordable-housing-bottleneck/) nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded and are sitting stalled because developers just can’t quite get enough money to build them. What would Prop. 1 do? If it passes, Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds to fund various types of housing, including homes for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. Where would the money go? Prop. 1 would fund a variety of programs. Here’s how it breaks down: $7.2 billion to buy, build or renovate apartment buildings, generally through low-interest loans to developers. Projects funded this way would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. Some would be used for “supportive housing,” homeless housing that includes additional services. This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. $1.25 billion to help veterans secure loans to buy homes. $1.1 billion to help low and moderate-income households buy homes. $500 million for the infrastructure that supports new housing construction, such as water, sewage, parks and transportation improvements. $450 million to build or renovate an estimated 2,500 units of farmworker housing. $350 million to fund affordable homes for an estimated 1,200 University of California and California State University students. $200 million in housing grants to tribes, which could fund both home construction and renovation. $200 million up for grabs to cities, counties and other groups that pitch pilot projects to develop low-cost housing. How would California pay for it? It would cost the state between $500 million and $600 million each year for about 25 years to repay the cost of the general housing bond, according to the legislative analyst. That money would come from the state’s general fund, and factors in interest. The $1.25 billion for veterans housing would not cost the state anything, as participating vets would pay it off through monthly loan payments. Have we done anything like this before? California voters approved (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2024/03/election-result-proposition-1/) (by the slimmest of margins) another bond (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/03/prop-1-update/) in 2024 that provided $2 billion to fund homes (https://calmatters.org/health/mental-health/2025/06/prop-1-mental-health-awards/) for people who need mental health and addiction services and veterans. That 2024 bond also was dubbed Prop. 1. What do supporters say? Supporters include housing developers and advocates, veterans groups, the California State University and University of California boards, groups representing California’s cities and counties, Democratic legislators and Gov. Gavin Newsom. Donors backing Prop. 1 also reflect some who would benefit. The campaign has received more than $12 million, including about $2 million from carpenters’ unions, $1 million from Airbnb and $1 million from Building a Better California, a PAC funded by Google founder Sergey Brin and other Silicon Valley billionaires. Sign up for free Δ Vivian Wan, chief executive of affordable housing provider Abode, says her organization has four projects with a planned total of about 230 units in the works that she hopes Prop. 1 will fund. Three are in the Bay Area and one is in Yolo County. Without that cash infusion, all four projects are stalled, she said. Projects for homeless and low-income residents need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset the cost of building. They often also have to fund additional services, such as case managers to help residents navigate their physical and mental health, addictions, finances and more. City and county dollars can pay for some but not all of that. Prop. 1 would be “huge,” Wan said. But it wouldn’t magically solve the housing crisis. “Is it enough? Absolutely not,” she said. “We are lightyears behind in terms of production to meet the need. We have underinvested in housing for decades. This is going to help, for sure, but we really need a permanent source.” What do opponents say? When this measure (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) came up for a floor vote before the Legislature, two Republican senators voted no, as well as seven Republican assemblymembers. Sen. Tony Strickland (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/legislators/tony-strickland-188489), a Republican from Huntington Beach who opposed the bill, said calling it “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026” amounted to a bait-and-switch maneuver, as only a small fraction of the total funds go to vets. “It really just says that you’re using veterans to pass your $10 billion general obligation bond,” he said during a June hearing. And, he said, there are better ways to get families into housing than using a bond to “borrow money against the future.” The strong revenues California experienced this year won’t continue, making it risky to push the state deeper into debt, he said. Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Housing Affordability
Proposition 1: Authorizes Bonds For Housing Affordability Programs. Legislative Statute.
Additional Titles
Cali fornia Proposition 1, Veteran and Housing Assistance Programs Bond Measure
Summary
Proposition 1 is a legislatively referred bond measure which was passed by the California Legislature on June 26, 2026, through Senate Bill 417 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (SB 417). Both the Assembly and Senate votes exceeded the two-thirds majority required for the Legislature to place a bond measure before voters. Because legislatively referred bond measures also require the governor’s approval, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s signature on SB 417 completed the process of placing Proposition 1 on the ballot.
Proposition 1 would allow California to sell $11.25 billion through state bonds for housing programs. Of that amount, $10 billion would go toward housing assistance for low- and moderate-income Californians that would be repaid by the General Fund, while $1.25 billion would support the state’s home loan program for veterans.
The $10 billion for housing would fund a range of projects, including affordable rental housing, assistance for first-time homebuyers, farmworker and student housing, housing infrastructure, tribal housing projects, and local pilot programs aimed at lowering housing costs.
F iscal Impact
(Summary of Legislative Analyst's Estimate of Net State and Local Government Fiscal Impact)
The state would repay the $10 billion housing portion from the General Fund, at an estimated cost of $500 million to $600 million a year for about 25 years. Veterans participating in the loan program would repay their home loans to the state. These payments are then used to pay back the bonds.
Because the state has to pay interest when it borrows money, the bond would cost about 15 percent more, after adjusting for inflation, than paying for the projects up front with money the state already has.
What your vote means (LAO's Analysis)
A YES vote on this measure means: The state could issue $11.25 billion in bonds to support housing programs for income-qualified Californians.
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not issue the proposed $11.25 billion in bonds for low-income housing programs.

Pro/Con Statements
Pro Con
Proponents argue that California’s housing affordability and homelessness crises require substantial public investment and that Proposition 1 would directly improve the lives of people struggling to find or keep stable housing. They contend that funding affordable housing construction and preservation, homeownership assistance, and housing for veterans, farmworkers, students, and homeless and foster youth would provide meaningful help to Californians most affected by high housing costs.
Opponents argue that California should not take on additional debt for housing when the state has substantial revenues and could fund these programs directly. They contend that the underlying housing problem is a shortage of available homes caused largely by regulations and development restrictions, rather than a lack of government spending on affordable housing.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Endorsement : Who should replace Nancy Pelosi in Congress? It’s not even a choice (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

I now have a good picture of the endorsements, so I'm going to check the Sacramento Bee/McClatchy and SF Chronicle editorials for their actual reasoning. The tally so far has the Bee and Chronicle backing Yes, while the East Bay Times, Mercury News, San Diego Union-Tribune, and Reason oppose it.

I'm going to look at the LAO's March 2026 report on streamlining the affordable housing funding system for its technical critique, along with the Enterprise Community Partners report on roughly 40,000 stalled units. After that I want the latest PPIC poll numbers, the Ballotpedia page, and a past-bond track record check.

I'm checking the date against the election: the East Bay Times page is dated November 2, 2026, and the Berkeley results page shows nothing certified yet, so the vote hasn't happened. I'll still run a quick search to confirm that before fetching the endorsements, the LAO report, the PPIC polls, Ballotpedia, and the budget brief.
Next I'm reading the pro-side editorials from the SF Chronicle and McClatchy, plus polling, Ballotpedia, and the LAO's March 2026 report that critics cite on the housing funding system.

Read McClatchy Media’s endorsement on California’s Proposition 1 | Opinion
By McClatchy Media’s California editorial board
Updated September 30, 2026 2:22 PM
A drone view of Mirasol Village on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. Proposition 1 looks to increase homebuilding in California through an $11.25 billion bond measure.
HECTOR AMEZCUA
hamezcua@sacbee.com
California has spent years creating laws that make it easier to build housing. Now it needs to help finance affordable housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026&utm_source=chatgpt.com) waiting to be produced at rents many Californians can afford.
There are nearly 40,000 affordable rental homes in the development pipeline (https://www.housingfinance.com/data-trends/california-pipeline-holds-nearly-40000-affordable-homes-seeking-funds) — designed and approved but awaiting sufficient financing to begin construction, according to Enterprise Community Partners, (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/about) a national housing nonprofit. Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html) could help close those financing gaps.
THE BEE’S VOTER GUIDE: Your guide to Proposition 1 (https://www.sacbee.com/news/politics-government/capitol-alert/article317117857.html)
A “yes” vote on Proposition 1 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_1,_Veteran_and_Housing_Assistance_Programs_Bond_Measure_(2026)) would authorize $11.25 billion in bonds: $10 billion for affordable housing and $1.25 billion for a longstandingCalVet home-loan program. (https://veteran.com/start/?src=adw&adg=185122315662&cmp=compterms&desc=calculator&matchtype=p&adid=803809597618&targetid=kwd-297340664879&label=&campaignid=23211217847&extid=&gad_source=1&gad_campaignid=23211217847&gbraid=0AAAAAqq9dHmkha--aWxuqkJFb13gc3lv2&gclid=CjwKCAjwq8PVBhAKEiwA2i3SHZePD1ETl_2tqMBf65xQCzjoSQ7GCNQ3Jj7lr4UZqy9t2I0slreQtBoCALsQAvD_BwE) Funds raised by Prop. 1 would support construction and preservation of affordable apartments (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/learning-center/resources/2026-california-affordable-housing-production-pipeline?utm_source=chatgpt.com), supportive housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing and infrastructure needed for affordable developments.
It’s undeniable that Californians struggle with rents they cannot afford, homelessness and home prices that put ownership beyond the reach of many working families.
Private developers generally cannot build housing for low-income and extremely low-income households and charge rents these families can afford while recovering the cost of construction. Every dollar the state invests leverages $4 from federal, local and private funding, according to the California Budget & Policy Center.
And taxpayers wouldn’t be purchasing a fleeting benefit. Affordable apartments receiving these subsidies generally must remain affordable for 55 years. Proponents estimate that turnover during that period could allow roughly 500,000 households to benefit.
There is a cost. TheLegislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/) estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing bond will cost the state’s General Fund $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years — roughly one-quarter of 1% of today’s General Fund budget. The separate $1.25 billion veterans portion is expected to be repaid through veterans’ mortgage payments, as previous CalVet bonds have been.
Opponents rightly say that housing in California is too expensive to build. But their argument that lawmakers should attack those costs instead of subsidizing affordable housing presents a false choice.
California can do both.
In just the past two legislative sessions, for instance, lawmakers have approved a series of changes to speed up environmental reviews and permitting, reduce some impact fees and simplify affordable-housing financing. The state’s newOne-Stop Shop financing reforms (https://ternercenter.berkeley.edu/research-and-policy/california-governors-budget-proposal-advances-a-one-stop-shop-for-affordable-housing/) and impact-fee changes alone are estimated by the Newsom administration to reduce affordable housing costs by $60,000-$70,000 per unit.
Government should eliminate unnecessary expenses, but it cannot eliminate the real costs of roads, schools, water, sewer and other infrastructure communities need as they grow. Nor is government responsible for every rising construction expense. Land, materials, interest rates, insurance, labor, contractor practices and other factors all contribute.
That’s why Proposition 1 should become something more than another infusion of money. California should use this enormous investment to learn precisely why affordable housing costs what it does.
For every project receiving bond money, the state should collect standardized information about land, construction, financing, permit and impact fees, professional services, labor expense, financing sources, approval times and change orders. This would allow researchers to compare similar projects being financed and determine why one costs $450,000 per unit while another costs $800,000 a unit.
And Californians should not have to become government accounting detectives to find the results.
The state should create a simple, prominently displayed public dashboard showing money awarded and spent, units produced and preserved, project locations, costs per unit and completion times. Proponents agreed with us that such transparency is achievable.
That need became obvious when we asked them what measurable results from California’s 2018 housing bond justify returning to voters for substantially more money. They cited strong demand and the fact that its funding was fully committed within five years, but could not readily provide the kind of statewide performance measures voters deserve.
Housing is fundamental to economic mobility. A family struggling to keep a roof over its head has little opportunity to save, educate its children, emphasize wellness or build financial security.
California needs those homes. It also needs to learn how to build the next ones faster and for less.
Proposition 1 gives California (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/) the opportunity to do better.
BEHIND THE STORY

Editorials represent the collective views of the editorial boards of McClatchy Media’s California opinion teams.
They do not reflect the individual opinions of board members or the views of reporters in the news sections of The Sacramento Bee and its sister publication, the San Luis Obispo Tribune. Reporters do not participate in editorial board deliberations or weigh in on board decisions.
In Sacramento, the board includes Executive Editor Chris Fusco, California Opinion Editor Marcos Breton, opinion writers Robin Epley, Tom Philp, LeBron Antonio Hill, Cathie Anderson and op-ed editor Hannah Holzer.
In San Luis Obispo, it includes Opinion Editor Stephanie Finucane.
We base our opinions on reporting by our colleagues in the news section, and our own reporting and interviews. Our members attend public meetings, call people and follow-up on story ideas from readers just as news reporters do.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Endorsement : Who should replace Nancy Pelosi in Congress? It’s not even a choice (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/scott-wiener-connie-chan-pelosi-22448323.php)
Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Rick M
Walnut Creek, CA
10/02/26
0
Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

In the interim, however, the need for more affordable housing is too desperate to wait. Prop 1 is well-positioned to reap the benefits of the state’s new streamlining laws. We recommend a yes vote.
