# Who gets the money
Applicants are nonprofit and for-profit developers, cities, counties and tribes. From 2019 to 2025, HCD funded 66,511 rental units . Of those, 26,904 (40%) are listed as completed so far , and 14,660 hadn't started construction. Projects funded in the last two or three years can't be finished yet, so the number to watch is whether the older awards close out. [21]
No single public database lists each HCD award with its developer, cost per unit and status. HCD's summary gives counts only. The best project-level records are CTCAC's staff reports, which list each tax-credit project's developer, units and total cost. [22]
# Red flags already on record
Fraud charges: Shangri-La Industries won about $115M in state Homekey contracts for about 500 homes. Its $27M Thousand Oaks project sits abandoned. Its former CFO was federally charged with mail fraud in Oct 2025 and has pleaded not guilty. [23] [17] The state, through Attorney General Bonta, sued the company in Jan 2024, alleging breach of contract and fraud. [24]
Close to home: San Bernardino's All Star Lodge, a Homekey motel conversion, was foreclosed after two years. No affordability restriction had been recorded, so the new owner could threaten big rent increases. [17] [25]
Homekey's record: $3.8B awarded since 2020. About 1 in 5 promised homes were unfinished at the end of 2024, and at least 10 awards (about 500 units) were canceled or clawed back. No state agency has publicly analyzed the program in detail. [17] This matters here because Prop 1's $1.15B supportive-housing share can fund the same kind of interim-to-permanent conversions. [8]
Audit advice ignored: In 2018 the State Auditor told the Legislature to require HCD to report every year on how it monitors bond programs, and to have its parent agency track HCD's progress. As of Jan 2026, the status of both is "No action taken." The audit's recommendations on HCD's administrative-cost overspending are still listed as only partially implemented or pending. [6]
Money lost, units unclear: A state committee let about $2.7B in housing bond authority expire in 2015–2017 without saying so publicly. The housing agencies don't share a project ID, so their unit counts may overlap. [26]
Evaluation blocked: AB 505 would have had the LAO evaluate Homekey. It died in the Assembly Housing Committee in Jan 2026 without a hearing. [27]
Not on the high-risk list: The State Auditor's Dec 2025 high-risk list doesn't include housing or homelessness spending. [28]
# Who to press, and what to ask for
Your Assemblymember and state Senator (look them up at findyourrep.legislature.ca.gov). Ask them to:
Pass the 2018 audit recommendation into law: public, project-by-project reporting for every Prop 1 award (developer, units, cost per unit, start and completion dates).
Ask the Joint Legislative Audit Committee to have the State Auditor audit the first round of Prop 1 awards. Any legislator can request an audit.
Bring back the Homekey evaluation that AB 505 proposed.
Lower the cost per unit: fund each project from fewer sources, since each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit [1] [15] , and adopt RAND's recommendations: a 30-day approval deadline, synchronized inspections, lower impact fees ($29,000 per unit in California vs. $12,000 in Colorado), and fewer design rules that don't affect safety. [3]
Treasurer and Controller candidates: they'll sit on CTCAC. Ask whether they'll score tax-credit applications on cost per unit and publish final costs for every finished project.
CTCAC and HCD meetings take public comment. Agendas are posted on the Treasurer's and HCD's websites.
Report waste or fraud to the State Auditor's whistleblower hotline: auditor.ca.gov/hotline or 800-952-5665. You can file anonymously. [29]
# Public records to request (CPRA)
The California Public Records Act is the state's version of FOIA. Anyone can file a request, and you don't need to give a reason. The agency must respond within 10 days, or within 24 days in unusual cases. [30] Send HCD requests through its online portal or to PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov (mailto:PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov). [31]
To HCD: Under the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code § 7920.000 et seq.), I request records sufficient to show, for every award made from Proposition 1 (2018) and Proposition 1 (2024) bond funds: project name, sponsor and developer, city, award amount and date, number of units, total development cost, and current status (not started, under construction, or completed, with the completion date). I also request any notices of default, recapture or cancellation for these awards. I prefer electronic records in their original format, such as a spreadsheet. Please state the estimated date the records will be available, as Gov. Code § 7922.535 requires.
To HCD: All monitoring reports, notices of default, and recapture or settlement records for Homekey projects sponsored by Shangri-La Industries, and for the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino.
To CTCAC (State Treasurer's Office): For every tax-credit project in San Bernardino County awarded from 2019 to 2025, the final cost certification showing the total development cost at completion, alongside the cost in the application.
What it does
$10B of the general-obligation bonds, repaid from the General Fund: $7.2B affordable rentals, $1.1B homeownership, $500M infrastructure, $450M farmworker housing, $350M UC/CSU student housing, $200M tribal housing, $200M local pilots. [2]
$1.25B CalVet home loans, repaid by veterans' loan payments (the program "has always operated at no direct cost to the state"). [2]
Cost: $500–600M a year for about 25 years. [2]
What we're not asking
Each bond is bigger and buys less. State housing bonds went $2.1B (2002), $2.85B (2006), $4B (2018), $11.25B (2026), while the cost of a tax-credit unit rose nearly 20% after inflation from 2019 to 2023. [9] [2] [1] Play it forward: a yes vote with no cost reform sets up a larger ask around 2030.
Subsidy chases a fixed pipeline. Most of these projects also need federal tax credits, which are capped. More state gap money doesn't add credits; it funds the same projects with one more layer, and each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The debt stacks. The state had $70.7B in general-obligation bonds outstanding and $39.9B authorized but unsold as of March 2026. Prop 1 adds $10B and Prop 38 another $8.4B, each costing $500–600M a year from the same General Fund that pays for schools and Medi-Cal. [16] [2]
Who checks year 30? Affordability covenants run for decades, but at the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino no covenant was even recorded. Nobody is funded to monitor covenants over the life of the bond. [17]
Game theory. Developers fund the campaign, win the awards, and fund the next bond. The Legislature can shift the split later by statute. HCD has no reason to fix its data when the money comes anyway. The bond vote is the only lever voters hold.
Better or worse in 20 years? Roughly 40,000 households housed, which is real. The cost structure, the data gap and the debt all stay. More units, same machine.
Open questions: Why does the bill cap nothing per unit? Where is the completed-unit count for the 2018 bond? Would a smaller bond tied to a cost cap have passed the Legislature?
Both sides
For: a real backlog of ready projects; rents are crushing low-income households; the bond funds farmworker, tribal and student housing that the market won't build.
Against: No official ballot argument against was filed. [32] Republican lawmakers, including Asm. Carl DeMaio, say only ~11% goes to veterans despite the name [12] , and that it borrows without addressing why building here costs so much [17] [33] ; RAND finds that at Colorado's costs, the same money would build 4x+ as many units. [3]

Yes $15.3M, No $0 in committees (through Oct 22). [7] Reform California has spent about $7,500 against. [12] Top Yes donors include Airbnb, two carpenters' union councils, and Building a Better California (funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr), at $1M each. [14]
Recipients are mostly nonprofit and for-profit affordable-housing developers, who apply to HCD and CalHFA. For example, MidPen Housing alone has 1,198 units waiting on state money. [15]
Supporters cite 461 "shovel-ready" projects (39,880 units) stalled for lack of gap funding. That count comes from Enterprise Community Partners, an affordable-housing finance group. [15]
# Does it solve a lasting problem?
It adds units, but it doesn't touch the cost per unit, which is the main reason each dollar builds so little. Every extra funding source a project needs adds about 4 months and ~$20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The state needs about 1 million lower-income units by 2030 under its own targets. This bond covers roughly 4% of that. [15] [2]
Our read is a toss-up. The backlog of ready projects is real and no one is organized against the bond. But the evidence on this page runs one way: cost per unit is the problem, the bond doesn't touch it, the agency has left the 2018 audit fixes untouched, and the campaign is funded by the applicants. Vote yes if you weigh the backlog more; vote no if you want the cost problem fixed first.
# If you vote yes: accountability
Bottom line: Most of the $10B goes out as competitive awards from one department (HCD) with no cost-per-unit limit in the law. The bill only requires an annual report (§ 54088), and it lets agencies write the program rules without the usual public rulemaking (§ 54077). [8] Watching how the money is spent is up to voters, reporters and the Legislature.
# Who spends it, and who answers for it
Money
Run by
Who's accountable
$7.2B rentals, $600M CalHome, $500M infill infrastructure, $450M farmworker, $200M tribal, $200M local pilots
HCD
HCD Director Gustavo Velasquez (since 2020) [18] ; Secretary Tomiquia Moss of the new California Housing and Homelessness Agency (since June 2026) [19] ; the Governor, who appoints both
$500M down-payment help
CalHFA
Executive Director Tony Sertich [20]
$350M student housing
UC and CSU
UC Regents and CSU Trustees

CalVet
An independent accountant must review the loan program every year while the bonds are outstanding. [8]
The tax credits most rentals also need
Tax Credit Allocation Committee (CTCAC)
Chaired by the State Treasurer. Other voting members: the Controller, the Finance Director, and the heads of HCD and CalHFA. [20] The Treasurer and Controller races are both on this ballot.
# Who gets the money
Applicants are nonprofit and for-profit developers, cities, counties and tribes. From 2019 to 2025, HCD funded 66,511 rental units . Of those, 26,904 (40%) are listed as completed so far , and 14,660 hadn't started construction. Projects funded in the last two or three years can't be finished yet, so the number to watch is whether the older awards close out. [21]
No single public database lists each HCD award with its developer, cost per unit and status. HCD's summary gives counts only. The best project-level records are CTCAC's staff reports, which list each tax-credit project's developer, units and total cost. [22]
# Red flags already on record
Fraud charges: Shangri-La Industries won about $115M in state Homekey contracts for about 500 homes. Its $27M Thousand Oaks project sits abandoned. Its former CFO was federally charged with mail fraud in Oct 2025 and has pleaded not guilty. [23] [17] The state, through Attorney General Bonta, sued the company in Jan 2024, alleging breach of contract and fraud. [24]
Close to home: San Bernardino's All Star Lodge, a Homekey motel conversion, was foreclosed after two years. No affordability restriction had been recorded, so the new owner could threaten big rent increases. [17] [25]
Homekey's record: $3.8B awarded since 2020. About 1 in 5 promised homes were unfinished at the end of 2024, and at least 10 awards (about 500 units) were canceled or clawed back. No state agency has publicly analyzed the program in detail. [17] This matters here because Prop 1's $1.15B supportive-housing share can fund the same kind of interim-to-permanent conversions. [8]
Audit advice ignored: In 2018 the State Auditor told the Legislature to require HCD to report every year on how it monitors bond programs, and to have its parent agency track HCD's progress. As of Jan 2026, the status of both is "No action taken." The audit's recommendations on HCD's administrative-cost overspending are still listed as only partially implemented or pending. [6]
Money lost, units unclear: A state committee let about $2.7B in housing bond authority expire in 2015–2017 without saying so publicly. The housing agencies don't share a project ID, so their unit counts may overlap. [26]
Evaluation blocked: AB 505 would have had the LAO evaluate Homekey. It died in the Assembly Housing Committee in Jan 2026 without a hearing. [27]
Not on the high-risk list: The State Auditor's Dec 2025 high-risk list doesn't include housing or homelessness spending. [28]
# Who to press, and what to ask for
Your Assemblymember and state Senator (look them up at findyourrep.legislature.ca.gov). Ask them to:
Pass the 2018 audit recommendation into law: public, project-by-project reporting for every Prop 1 award (developer, units, cost per unit, start and completion dates).
Ask the Joint Legislative Audit Committee to have the State Auditor audit the first round of Prop 1 awards. Any legislator can request an audit.
Bring back the Homekey evaluation that AB 505 proposed.
Lower the cost per unit: fund each project from fewer sources, since each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit [1] [15] , and adopt RAND's recommendations: a 30-day approval deadline, synchronized inspections, lower impact fees ($29,000 per unit in California vs. $12,000 in Colorado), and fewer design rules that don't affect safety. [3]
Treasurer and Controller candidates: they'll sit on CTCAC. Ask whether they'll score tax-credit applications on cost per unit and publish final costs for every finished project.
CTCAC and HCD meetings take public comment. Agendas are posted on the Treasurer's and HCD's websites.
Report waste or fraud to the State Auditor's whistleblower hotline: auditor.ca.gov/hotline or 800-952-5665. You can file anonymously. [29]
# Public records to request (CPRA)
The California Public Records Act is the state's version of FOIA. Anyone can file a request, and you don't need to give a reason. The agency must respond within 10 days, or within 24 days in unusual cases. [30] Send HCD requests through its online portal or to PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov (mailto:PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov). [31]
To HCD: Under the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code § 7920.000 et seq.), I request records sufficient to show, for every award made from Proposition 1 (2018) and Proposition 1 (2024) bond funds: project name, sponsor and developer, city, award amount and date, number of units, total development cost, and current status (not started, under construction, or completed, with the completion date). I also request any notices of default, recapture or cancellation for these awards. I prefer electronic records in their original format, such as a spreadsheet. Please state the estimated date the records will be available, as Gov. Code § 7922.535 requires.
To HCD: All monitoring reports, notices of default, and recapture or settlement records for Homekey projects sponsored by Shangri-La Industries, and for the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino.
To CTCAC (State Treasurer's Office): For every tax-credit project in San Bernardino County awarded from 2019 to 2025, the final cost certification showing the total development cost at completion, alongside the cost in the application.
What it does
$10B of the general-obligation bonds, repaid from the General Fund: $7.2B affordable rentals, $1.1B homeownership, $500M infrastructure, $450M farmworker housing, $350M UC/CSU student housing, $200M tribal housing, $200M local pilots. [2]
$1.25B CalVet home loans, repaid by veterans' loan payments (the program "has always operated at no direct cost to the state"). [2]
Cost: $500–600M a year for about 25 years. [2]
What we're not asking
Each bond is bigger and buys less. State housing bonds went $2.1B (2002), $2.85B (2006), $4B (2018), $11.25B (2026), while the cost of a tax-credit unit rose nearly 20% after inflation from 2019 to 2023. [9] [2] [1] Play it forward: a yes vote with no cost reform sets up a larger ask around 2030.
Subsidy chases a fixed pipeline. Most of these projects also need federal tax credits, which are capped. More state gap money doesn't add credits; it funds the same projects with one more layer, and each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The debt stacks. The state had $70.7B in general-obligation bonds outstanding and $39.9B authorized but unsold as of March 2026. Prop 1 adds $10B and Prop 38 another $8.4B, each costing $500–600M a year from the same General Fund that pays for schools and Medi-Cal. [16] [2]
Who checks year 30? Affordability covenants run for decades, but at the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino no covenant was even recorded. Nobody is funded to monitor covenants over the life of the bond. [17]
Game theory. Developers fund the campaign, win the awards, and fund the next bond. The Legislature can shift the split later by statute. HCD has no reason to fix its data when the money comes anyway. The bond vote is the only lever voters hold.
Better or worse in 20 years? Roughly 40,000 households housed, which is real. The cost structure, the data gap and the debt all stay. More units, same machine.
Open questions: Why does the bill cap nothing per unit? Where is the completed-unit count for the 2018 bond? Would a smaller bond tied to a cost cap have passed the Legislature?
Both sides
For: a real backlog of ready projects; rents are crushing low-income households; the bond funds farmworker, tribal and student housing that the market won't build.
Against: No official ballot argument against was filed. [32] Republican lawmakers, including Asm. Carl DeMaio, say only ~11% goes to veterans despite the name [12] , and that it borrows without addressing why building here costs so much [17] [33] ; RAND finds that at Colorado's costs, the same money would build 4x+ as many units. [3]

I'm weighing a 2018 bond track record: SPUR reports 22,735 housing units produced by the time the Prop 1 funds ran out in FY 2023–24, and a separate figure has HCD funding 66,511 rental units from 2019 to 2025, with about 40% of those listed as completed so far.

I'm weighing the SPUR figure of 22,735 units produced against the LAO's earlier estimate, and I'm not sure they measure the same thing. The californiapeople.org number covers all HCD funding, not only the 2018 bond, and I can't confirm how "produced" is defined. Rather than lean on shaky numbers, I'm thinking about pulling the full SPUR and californiapeople.org pages to check their exact claims.

content.text: The 2018 bond's track record matters for how much weight to give the supporters' claims. I'll check both sources that report numbers on it.

CA
Prop
1
|
Bond
Authorizes Bonds for Housing Affordability Programs
Authorizes $10 billion in general obligation bonds to fund production of affordable and supportive housing and $1.25 billion in mortgage revenue bonds to fund a homeownership program for veterans and military families.
SPUR's Recommendation
California’s housing affordability crisis continues to worsen, largely because of a supply shortage and inadequate funding to build more. Even with lower construction costs, affordable housing construction and preservation would still require significant, consistent government subsidies. Thousands of approved affordable housing projects have stalled because of a lack of financing.
General obligation bonds are needed periodically to replenish funding for the state’s main affordable housing finance programs. Prop. 1’s proposed bond funds pair with state and federal Low Income Housing Tax Credits to finance affordable housing developments. This measure is critical to expanding affordable housing opportunities for lower-income residents across California through new construction, preservation, and homebuyer assistance. Funds would be distributed through well-established state programs with a proven track record of success.
Vote YES
What Prop. 1 Would Do
According to the California Housing Partnership, Proposition 1 will help finance more than 40,000 shovel-ready affordable rental homes and help 20,000 California households attain homeownership. 1 The bond proceeds would replenish key long-standing state affordable housing financing programs and be allocated as follows:
$5.10 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program. At least 10% of units in each development receiving these funds must be affordable to extremely low-income households.
$1.25 billion in self-supporting revenue bonds for the CalVet Home Loan Program to help veterans and military families buy a home. These bonds are repaid entirely through mortgage payments and do not rely on taxpayer funding.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing administered through the Multifamily Housing Program. The program requires funding to create a reserve account to cover operating deficits for developments receiving funding.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded multifamily rental housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$600 million for the CalHOME Program for new construction of affordable ownership homes.
$500 million for the My Home down payment assistance program for lower- and moderate-income households.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program of 2019 for grants supporting infrastructure needed to support developing affordable and mixed-income housing in infill locations.
$450 million to the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for new affordable student housing projects split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program to finance housing and housing-related activities enabling tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million for a program to be created by the Legislature that funds acquisition and rehabilitation of unrestricted housing units (i.e., unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable) and the attachment of long-term affordability restrictions to the units.
$200 million to the Local Housing Trust Fund Program to fund competitive grants and loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or create or preserve affordable housing.
The Backstory
The state has historically used voter-approved general obligation bonds to fund affordable housing programs. In 2018, voters approved Proposition 1, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2018, which provided $4 billion in funding, including $1 billion for the Department of Veterans Affairs program and $3 billion for various affordable housing programs. As of fiscal year 2023–24, when the 2018 Prop. 1 bond funding ran out, 22,735 units of housing had been produced.
Enterprise Community Partners’ 2026 California Affordable Housing Production Pipeline report, released in March, found that nearly 40,000 approved affordable housing units are frozen due to a lack of funding and could be built with this new financing source. 2
The proposed bond has undergone a rigorous process and has broad support. Over the past four years, the Legislature has introduced various affordable housing bond measures, including bills by Assemblymember Wicks and Senator Cabaldon. Those bills have moved through the legislative process over the past year and a half, giving the members of the Legislature multiple opportunities to negotiate the terms. Governor Newsom, Senate President Pro Tem Limón, and Assembly Speaker Rivas negotiated final amendments for the authorizing legislation, SB 417, the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026. The State Legislature voted with supermajorities in each house to place the proposition on the November 2026 ballot.
Legislative analyses of the measure find the total cost to pay off the bonds would be approximately $17.39 billion in principal and interest. Average annual debt service payments from the State’s General Fund are estimated at approximately $580 million when all bonds are sold, assuming an interest rate of 4.02% and a 30-year maturity. This amount of annual debt service represents about 0.26% of the State’s General Fund budget.
According to the State of California Debt Affordability Report issued by the state treasurer in October 2025, California’s ratio of General Fund-supported debt service to General Fund revenues was 3.59% in fiscal year 2024–25 and was estimated to be 3.95% in fiscal year 2025–26 . 3 This ratio is in line with the 4% historical average for bonded indebtedness.
A simple majority (50% plus one vote) of California voters is required to pass Prop. 1.
Equity Impacts
The Bay Area Equity Atlas finds that all nine Bay Area counties struggle to come anywhere close to meeting their state-mandated share of new housing construction. In 2023 and 2024, the Bay Area permitted just 9% of its required units, including only 5% of required very-low-income units and 10% of required low-income units. 4
This lack of affordable housing options increases displacement pressures on lower-income households and households of color. The Bay Area Equity Atlas’s Black Communities and the Bay Area's Housing Crisis report, published in April 2025, found the Bay Area lost more than 5,000 Black-owned households during the 2010s, with significant declines in historic Black communities in the East Bay, San Francisco, and Solano County, while the number of Black renter households increased by just 300. 5
Sufficient funding to create below-market-rate rental and homeownership opportunities will help address the affordability challenges and displacement pressures faced by lower-income households, Black households, and other households of color.
Pros
The state faces a chronic affordable housing crisis that cannot be addressed without significant ongoing public investment to lower housing costs for lower-income households.
The bond would make the most of recent federal changes to the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit program that allow California to nearly double its affordable housing production: if the state invests $4.1 billion annually, it can leverage $6.7 billion in available federal funding.
The funding would be distributed through existing state programs with a proven track record of producing affordable housing options for lower-income residents.
The Bay Area is well positioned to use the funds effectively, given the number of highly effective nonprofit affordable housing developers here.
Con
The bond would contribute to the state’s debt burden, with debt service on the bond representing 0.26% of the overall State General Fund budget.
Vote YES

# Key findings
A subsidized apartment built with California tax credits cost about $630,000 per unit in 2023, up nearly 20% since 2019 after inflation. [1]
The state's share in this bond works out to roughly $180,000 per rental unit ($7.2B for up to 40,000 units, our math). The rest has to come from tax credits and local money. [2]
RAND estimates that at Colorado's cost levels, about $1.25B of recent spending by California's four biggest housing programs would have built more than 4 times as many units . [3]
The State Auditor has flagged the agency that runs these bonds (HCD) in five audits (2007–2018) : weak monitoring, unexplained high per-unit costs, and a data system that never worked fully. [4] [5] [6]
The campaign is funded mostly by the groups that would apply for the money: $13.9M of $15.3M came from a committee sponsored by affordable-housing organizations. [7]
The split you vote on isn't fixed. The bond act lets the Legislature "amend this chapter in order to reallocate the proceeds" among its programs by ordinary statute, with no further vote of the people. [8]

Audit pattern: In 2014 the State Auditor found that 7 of 10 sampled projects cost well above local averages with no documented justification. The auditor also found a $1.35M grant for an outdoor "green living room" that built no housing, $486M still waiting to be awarded, and HCD's cost benchmarks hadn't been updated since 2008. [4]
# Money and conflicts
Yes $15.3M, No $0 in committees (through Oct 22). [7] Reform California has spent about $7,500 against. [12] Top Yes donors include Airbnb, two carpenters' union councils, and Building a Better California (funded by Sergey Brin and John Doerr), at $1M each. [14]
Recipients are mostly nonprofit and for-profit affordable-housing developers, who apply to HCD and CalHFA. For example, MidPen Housing alone has 1,198 units waiting on state money. [15]
Supporters cite 461 "shovel-ready" projects (39,880 units) stalled for lack of gap funding. That count comes from Enterprise Community Partners, an affordable-housing finance group. [15]
# Does it solve a lasting problem?
It adds units, but it doesn't touch the cost per unit, which is the main reason each dollar builds so little. Every extra funding source a project needs adds about 4 months and ~$20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The state needs about 1 million lower-income units by 2030 under its own targets. This bond covers roughly 4% of that. [15] [2]
Our read is a toss-up. The backlog of ready projects is real and no one is organized against the bond. But the evidence on this page runs one way: cost per unit is the problem, the bond doesn't touch it, the agency has left the 2018 audit fixes untouched, and the campaign is funded by the applicants. Vote yes if you weigh the backlog more; vote no if you want the cost problem fixed first.
# If you vote yes: accountability
Bottom line: Most of the $10B goes out as competitive awards from one department (HCD) with no cost-per-unit limit in the law. The bill only requires an annual report (§ 54088), and it lets agencies write the program rules without the usual public rulemaking (§ 54077). [8] Watching how the money is spent is up to voters, reporters and the Legislature.

# Who gets the money
Applicants are nonprofit and for-profit developers, cities, counties and tribes. From 2019 to 2025, HCD funded 66,511 rental units . Of those, 26,904 (40%) are listed as completed so far , and 14,660 hadn't started construction. Projects funded in the last two or three years can't be finished yet, so the number to watch is whether the older awards close out. [21]
No single public database lists each HCD award with its developer, cost per unit and status. HCD's summary gives counts only. The best project-level records are CTCAC's staff reports, which list each tax-credit project's developer, units and total cost. [22]
# Red flags already on record
Fraud charges: Shangri-La Industries won about $115M in state Homekey contracts for about 500 homes. Its $27M Thousand Oaks project sits abandoned. Its former CFO was federally charged with mail fraud in Oct 2025 and has pleaded not guilty. [23] [17] The state, through Attorney General Bonta, sued the company in Jan 2024, alleging breach of contract and fraud. [24]
Close to home: San Bernardino's All Star Lodge, a Homekey motel conversion, was foreclosed after two years. No affordability restriction had been recorded, so the new owner could threaten big rent increases. [17] [25]
Homekey's record: $3.8B awarded since 2020. About 1 in 5 promised homes were unfinished at the end of 2024, and at least 10 awards (about 500 units) were canceled or clawed back. No state agency has publicly analyzed the program in detail. [17] This matters here because Prop 1's $1.15B supportive-housing share can fund the same kind of interim-to-permanent conversions. [8]
Audit advice ignored: In 2018 the State Auditor told the Legislature to require HCD to report every year on how it monitors bond programs, and to have its parent agency track HCD's progress. As of Jan 2026, the status of both is "No action taken." The audit's recommendations on HCD's administrative-cost overspending are still listed as only partially implemented or pending. [6]
Money lost, units unclear: A state committee let about $2.7B in housing bond authority expire in 2015–2017 without saying so publicly. The housing agencies don't share a project ID, so their unit counts may overlap. [26]
Evaluation blocked: AB 505 would have had the LAO evaluate Homekey. It died in the Assembly Housing Committee in Jan 2026 without a hearing. [27]
Not on the high-risk list: The State Auditor's Dec 2025 high-risk list doesn't include housing or homelessness spending. [28]
# Who to press, and what to ask for
Your Assemblymember and state Senator (look them up at findyourrep.legislature.ca.gov). Ask them to:
Pass the 2018 audit recommendation into law: public, project-by-project reporting for every Prop 1 award (developer, units, cost per unit, start and completion dates).
Ask the Joint Legislative Audit Committee to have the State Auditor audit the first round of Prop 1 awards. Any legislator can request an audit.
Bring back the Homekey evaluation that AB 505 proposed.
Lower the cost per unit: fund each project from fewer sources, since each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit [1] [15] , and adopt RAND's recommendations: a 30-day approval deadline, synchronized inspections, lower impact fees ($29,000 per unit in California vs. $12,000 in Colorado), and fewer design rules that don't affect safety. [3]
Treasurer and Controller candidates: they'll sit on CTCAC. Ask whether they'll score tax-credit applications on cost per unit and publish final costs for every finished project.
CTCAC and HCD meetings take public comment. Agendas are posted on the Treasurer's and HCD's websites.
Report waste or fraud to the State Auditor's whistleblower hotline: auditor.ca.gov/hotline or 800-952-5665. You can file anonymously. [29]
# Public records to request (CPRA)
The California Public Records Act is the state's version of FOIA. Anyone can file a request, and you don't need to give a reason. The agency must respond within 10 days, or within 24 days in unusual cases. [30] Send HCD requests through its online portal or to PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov (mailto:PRARequest@hcd.ca.gov). [31]
To HCD: Under the California Public Records Act (Gov. Code § 7920.000 et seq.), I request records sufficient to show, for every award made from Proposition 1 (2018) and Proposition 1 (2024) bond funds: project name, sponsor and developer, city, award amount and date, number of units, total development cost, and current status (not started, under construction, or completed, with the completion date). I also request any notices of default, recapture or cancellation for these awards. I prefer electronic records in their original format, such as a spreadsheet. Please state the estimated date the records will be available, as Gov. Code § 7922.535 requires.
To HCD: All monitoring reports, notices of default, and recapture or settlement records for Homekey projects sponsored by Shangri-La Industries, and for the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino.
To CTCAC (State Treasurer's Office): For every tax-credit project in San Bernardino County awarded from 2019 to 2025, the final cost certification showing the total development cost at completion, alongside the cost in the application.
What it does
$10B of the general-obligation bonds, repaid from the General Fund: $7.2B affordable rentals, $1.1B homeownership, $500M infrastructure, $450M farmworker housing, $350M UC/CSU student housing, $200M tribal housing, $200M local pilots. [2]
$1.25B CalVet home loans, repaid by veterans' loan payments (the program "has always operated at no direct cost to the state"). [2]
Cost: $500–600M a year for about 25 years. [2]
What we're not asking
Each bond is bigger and buys less. State housing bonds went $2.1B (2002), $2.85B (2006), $4B (2018), $11.25B (2026), while the cost of a tax-credit unit rose nearly 20% after inflation from 2019 to 2023. [9] [2] [1] Play it forward: a yes vote with no cost reform sets up a larger ask around 2030.
Subsidy chases a fixed pipeline. Most of these projects also need federal tax credits, which are capped. More state gap money doesn't add credits; it funds the same projects with one more layer, and each extra source adds about 4 months and $20,460 per unit. [1] [15]
The debt stacks. The state had $70.7B in general-obligation bonds outstanding and $39.9B authorized but unsold as of March 2026. Prop 1 adds $10B and Prop 38 another $8.4B, each costing $500–600M a year from the same General Fund that pays for schools and Medi-Cal. [16] [2]
Who checks year 30? Affordability covenants run for decades, but at the All Star Lodge in San Bernardino no covenant was even recorded. Nobody is funded to monitor covenants over the life of the bond. [17]
Game theory. Developers fund the campaign, win the awards, and fund the next bond. The Legislature can shift the split later by statute. HCD has no reason to fix its data when the money comes anyway. The bond vote is the only lever voters hold.
Better or worse in 20 years? Roughly 40,000 households housed, which is real. The cost structure, the data gap and the debt all stay. More units, same machine.
Open questions: Why does the bill cap nothing per unit? Where is the completed-unit count for the 2018 bond? Would a smaller bond tied to a cost cap have passed the Legislature?
Both sides
For: a real backlog of ready projects; rents are crushing low-income households; the bond funds farmworker, tribal and student housing that the market won't build.
Against: No official ballot argument against was filed. [32] Republican lawmakers, including Asm. Carl DeMaio, say only ~11% goes to veterans despite the name [12] , and that it borrows without addressing why building here costs so much [17] [33] ; RAND finds that at Colorado's costs, the same money would build 4x+ as many units. assistantMessageEvent.content:
I won't give a bare yes or no. I read the official guide, the LAO analysis, the bill text, and coverage and editorials from both sides. The facts are fairly clear, and what's left is a values call between long-term debt and a real funding gap for affordable housing. I don't think I should make that call for you.

**What Prop 1 does**
- It lets the state borrow $11.25B. Of that, $10B is repaid from the General Fund. Most of it ($7.2B) goes to affordable rental construction and rehab, and the rest to homebuyer help, farmworker, student and tribal housing, and infrastructure. The other $1.25B funds CalVet home loans that veterans repay themselves.
- The nonpartisan LAO says repayment costs the General Fund $500–600M a year for about 25 years, roughly 0.25% of the budget. That is about 15% more than paying cash, adjusted for inflation.
- The LAO says the bond subsidizes up to 40,000 rental units, about 2,500 farmworker units and about 1,200 student beds. It also helps up to 40,000 households toward homeownership.

**Strongest case for Yes**
- The 2018 housing bond is fully committed, and the state's main rental program gets about $9 in requests per $1 available.
- An industry report counts roughly 40,000 permitted affordable units stalled for lack of gap financing. This year's budget put only $200M of new cash into that program.
- Funded units must stay income-restricted for 55 years. Supporters say each state dollar draws about $4 in other money, which is their estimate.
- Backers include Newsom, the Democratic Party, veterans and housing groups, and California YIMBY, a pro-construction group. The SF Chronicle and Sacramento Bee editorial boards say yes. The Bee wants a public cost-per-unit dashboard.

**Strongest case for No**
- It is a 25-year claim on the budget. The LAO projected deficits of $20–35B a year as of January.
- Cost estimates vary. Howard Jarvis says taxpayers repay "roughly double." The Budget Center puts nominal repayment at about $17.4B on $10B. The LAO's inflation-adjusted premium is 15%.
- It doesn't address construction costs. RAND found subsidized affordable housing in California costs about 1.5× market-rate housing here. It cites above-market wage requirements and design-related fees. Forty thousand units is about 4% of the roughly 1 million affordable homes the state says it needs.
- Only 11% goes to veterans, despite the name. The bill's accountability chapter is one annual-report requirement, which supporters call "strict accountability." When the Bee asked, proponents couldn't readily show statewide results from the 2018 bond.
- Howard Jarvis, CalTax, and the Mercury News/East Bay Times editorial boards oppose it. Nine legislators, all Republicans, voted no.

**Where things stand:** There is no organized opposition campaign, and the Yes side has raised more than $12M. PPIC's Oct. 16–22 poll showed 60–38 yes among likely voters. Election Day is Nov. 3, and polls close at 8 p.m.

**How to decide**
Both sides agree the bond doesn't fix construction costs. They disagree on whether that matters. Supporters say "California can do both," meaning fund subsidies now and fix costs too. Critics say the money should wait until costs come down.
- **Lean yes** if you think subsidized low-income housing is worth the cost and a bond is the practical way to pay for it, given the backlog and the lack of other funding.
- **Lean no** if you'd rather not add long-term debt during deficits, want cost and permitting reform first, or want this spending to compete in the annual budget.

If you tell me which of these matter most to you, I'll tell you which way they point.

Sources: [Voter guide](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/), [LAO](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026), [CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/), [Budget Center](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/), [SPUR (yes)](https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-1-affordable-housing-bond), [CA YIMBY (yes)](https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-1-2026/), [Sacramento Bee (yes)](https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html), [HJTA (no)](https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/), [Mercury News/East Bay Times (no)](https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/), [RAND](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3743-1.html), [PPIC](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/)

- Backers include Newsom, the Democratic Party, veterans and housing groups, and California YIMBY, a pro-construction group. The SF Chronicle and Sacramento Bee editorial boards say yes. The Bee wants a public cost-per-unit dashboard.

**Strongest case for No**
- It is a 25-year claim on the budget. The LAO projected deficits of $20–35B a year as of January.
- Cost estimates vary. Howard Jarvis says taxpayers repay "roughly double." The Budget Center puts nominal repayment at about $17.4B on $10B. The LAO's inflation-adjusted premium is 15%.
- It doesn't address construction costs. RAND found subsidized affordable housing in California costs about 1.5× market-rate housing here. It cites above-market wage requirements and design-related fees. Forty thousand units is about 4% of the roughly 1 million affordable homes the state says it needs.
- Only 11% goes to veterans, despite the name. The bill's accountability chapter is one annual-report requirement, which supporters call "strict accountability." When the Bee asked, proponents couldn't readily show statewide results from the 2018 bond.
- Howard Jarvis, CalTax, and the Mercury News/East Bay Times editorial boards oppose it. Nine legislators, all Republicans, voted no.

**Where things stand:** There is no organized opposition campaign, and the Yes side has raised more than $12M. PPIC's Oct. 16–22 poll showed 60–38 yes among likely voters. Election Day is Nov. 3, and polls close at 8 p.m.

**How to decide**
Both sides agree the bond doesn't fix construction costs. They disagree on whether that matters. Supporters say "California can do both," meaning fund subsidies now and fix costs too. Critics say the money should wait until costs come down.
- **Lean yes** if you think subsidized low-income housing is worth the cost and a bond is the practical way to pay for it, given the backlog and the lack of other funding.
- **Lean no** if you'd rather not add long-term debt during deficits, want cost and permitting reform first, or want this spending to compete in the annual budget.

If you tell me which of these matter most to you, I'll tell you which way they point.

Sources: [Voter guide](https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/propositions/1/), [LAO](https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026), [CalMatters](https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/), [Budget Center](https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/), [SPUR (yes)](https://www.spur.org/voter-guide/2026-11/ca-prop-1-affordable-housing-bond), [CA YIMBY (yes)](https://cayimby.org/blog/proposition-1-2026/), [Sacramento Bee (yes)](https://www.sacbee.com/opinion/article317326136.html), [HJTA (no)](https://www.hjta.org/2026votingguide/), [Mercury News/East Bay Times (no)](https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2026/10/26/endorsement-proposition-1-37-affordable-housing-crisis-november-3-general-election/), [RAND](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA3743-1.html), [PPIC](https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/)

PROP
1
AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Public Sector Funds Some Home Building. In most years, about 100,000 houses and apartments are built in California. Most of these housing units are built entirely with private dollars. Some, however, receive financial help from federal, state, or local governments. In the case of housing funded by the state, the state government generally provides local governments, nonprofit organizations, and private developers with grants or low-cost loans to fund a portion of the housing units’ construction costs. Typically, housing built with these funds must be sold or rented to Californians with low incomes.
Bonds Are a Common Way for the State to Fund Home Building and Homeownership Programs. Over the past few decades, the state has used general obligation bonds to fund various housing programs. Bonds are a way the state borrows money to cover the up-front costs of a development and then repays the money plus interest over time. The last statewide general obligation bond for affordable housing was approved by voters in 2024, providing $2 billion to provide housing for veterans and other people with mental health or substance use challenges who are facing homelessness.
Home Loan Program for Veterans. The state’s veterans home loan program provides home loans to eligible veterans, including veterans who may not otherwise qualify for a home loan. Under the program, the state sells general obligation bonds to investors and uses the funds to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. Participating veterans repay the cost of the bonds through their payments on their home loan. The last statewide general obligation bond for veterans home loans was approved by voters in 2018, which provided $1 billion for the program.
PROPOSAL
New General Obligation Bond for Housing. Proposition 1 allows the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds for housing purposes. This amount consists of (1) a $10 billion bond for a variety of state housing programs that would be repaid by the General Fund and (2) a $1.25 billion bond that would be repaid by veterans’ payments on their home loans. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons. For more information on the state’s General Fund-supported bonds, please see “Overview of State Bond Debt” later in this guide.)
State Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides bond funding for various types of housing programs, which are summarized in Figure 1. The funds would be allocated over a number of years. The major categories of housing programs supported by the bond are:
Affordable Multifamily Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $7.2 billion to acquire, build, or renovate rental housing, such as apartment buildings&#46 These programs generally provide local governments and private developers with low-interest loans to fund part of the project cost. In exchange, projects generally must reserve units for low-income households for a period of 55 years. Some of this funding would be used for supportive housing, which provides on-site service (such as mental health and substance use counseling) to certain residents.
Homeownership Programs. Proposition 1 provides $1.1 billion to support homeownership for low- and moderate-income households. Some of the funds would be used to provide homebuying assistance for first-time homebuyers through loans that generally do not have to be paid back until the home is sold or paid off. Other funds would be provided to nonprofit organizations and other entities for activities such as acquiring land to build homes for eligible low-income homebuyers and repairing existing homes owned by low-income households.
Infrastructure Programs. Proposition 1 provides $500 million for a variety of infrastructure projects to support affordable housing developments, such as water, sewage, parks, and transportation improvements.
Farmworker Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $450 million in loans and grants to build or renovate housing for farmworkers. Program funds could be used for both rental and owner-occupied housing.
Higher Education Student Housing Programs. Proposition 1 provides $350 million, split evenly between the University of California and California State University, for affordable student housing.
Tribal Housing Program. Proposition 1 provides $200 million in grants to tribes. Funds could be used for various housing-related purposes, including construction and repair of rental and owner-occupied housing.
Local Pilot Programs. Proposition 1 provides $200 million that would be available to cities, counties, and certain other entities for pilot projects aimed at developing housing at reduced costs.
Veterans Housing Program. Proposition 1 also provides $1.25 billion for home loan assistance to veterans. Veterans generally use these loans to purchase single-family residences, condominiums, farms, and mobile homes.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Increased State Cost to Repay the $10 Billion Bond for Housing Programs. The state General Fund cost to repay the bond would be $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years . The estimated annual cost would be about one-quarter of 1 percent (0.25 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. Since the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, the total cost of the bond would be about 15 percent more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
No Direct State Cost for Veterans Housing Program. Veterans participating in the home loan program would make monthly payments to the state, allowing the state to repay the bonds. These payments have always covered the amount owed on the bonds, meaning the program has always operated at no direct cost to the state.
Administrative Costs. A number of state entities would experience increased costs to administer the various housing programs. A portion of the bond funds would cover these costs.
Impact of Funds. Much of the funding from Proposition 1 would be used together with other government monies to provide housing assistance. The bond funds would provide subsidies for up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, as well as about 2,500 units for farmworkers and about 1,200 beds for university students. The funds also would help up to 40,000 households, including about 2,100 veterans, with homeownership by providing homebuyer assistance and supporting the production and repair of homes.

AUTHORIZES BONDS FOR HOUSING AFFORDABILITY PROGRAMS. LEGISLATIVE STATUTE.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 1
YES ON PROP. 1: AFFORDABLE HOMES FOR VETERANS, SENIORS, PEOPLE WITH DISABILITIES AND WORKING FAMILIES-WITHOUT RAISING TAXES
All Californians deserve a safe and affordable place to call home, but California has a housing shortage that is driving the nation’s worst housing affordability crisis. More than half of renters spend over 30% of their income on rent and only 22% of households can afford a median-priced home, yet only 1% of California’s state budget goes to housing.
Prop. 1 gives Californians the opportunity to:
Fast-track housing production;
Provide housing to working families, veterans, people with disabilities and seniors;
Help prevent homelessness by keeping our most vulnerable neighbors in their homes;
Expands homeownership opportunities;
Maintains strict fiscal accountability and transparency with NO NEW TAXES.
PROP. 1 HONORS OUR VETERANS
Dedicates $1.25 billion solely to veterans’ housing and homeownership opportunities through the existing CalVet Home Loan Program, which has already helped almost a million veterans and their families.
“California has one of the largest populations of homeless veterans in the nation. After their service, our veterans deserve a place to call home. Prop. 1 delivers on that promise.”-Michael Blecker, President, CA Association of Veteran Service Agencies
PROP. 1 BUILDS HOMES LOW- AND MIDDLE-INCOME FAMILIES CAN AFFORD
Prop. 1 jumpstarts the construction of tens of thousands of shovel-ready affordable homes across California, quickly turning stalled construction into move-in ready homes. The teacher in your child’s classroom, the firefighter who protects your neighborhood, first-time homebuyers, low- and middle-income Californians, and the nurse at your local hospital can no longer afford to live in most California communities. Prop. 1 builds more homes working people can actually afford.
NO NEW TAXES-STRICT ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY
Prop. 1 doesn’t raise taxes and every dollar comes with strict accountability and public reporting. Voters will be able to see exactly how many homes get built, where, and at what cost. Prop. 1 unlocks federal matching funds, bringing tax dollars we send to Washington back home to California.
PROP. 1 HELPS SENIORS, VETERANS & OUR MOST VULNERABLE
Prop. 1 creates and preserves housing to help those who are one crisis away from homelessness stay off the streets, low-income seniors on fixed incomes, survivors of domestic violence and their families, veterans, at risk and foster youth, and people with disabilities who all deserve safe and stable homes.
PROP. 1 INVESTS IN COMMUNITIES & ESSENTIAL WORKERS
Quality, affordable housing is the foundation of thriving communities. Prop. 1 strengthens that foundation by helping essential workers-from firefighters and teachers to nurses-afford to live in the communities they serve. Working families and essential workers across California are being priced out and left behind. Prop. 1 enables the construction of affordable housing for these essential workers who dedicate their lives to our communities.
YES ON PROP. 1: SUPPORTED BY VETERANS, SENIORS, TEACHERS, FIREFIGHTERS, AND AFFORDABLE HOUSING ADVOCATES including Habitat for Humanity California, California Alliance for Retired Americans, Housing California, California Housing Consortium, California Alliance of Child and Family Services.
VOTE YES ON PROP. 1, Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond, to honor those veterans who served; provide safe and stable housing to California’s most vulnerable; guarantee strict fiscal accountability with no new taxes; and build the affordable homes all Californians deserve.

PREPARED BY THE ATTORNEY GENERAL

$5.1 billion to build and rehabilitate multifamily rental housing;
$2.1 billion to acquire, rehabilitate, or preserve affordable housing units, and provide supportive housing for those experiencing homelessness;
$1.25 billion for state-funded mortgages for California veterans;
$1.1 billion for homeownership and downpayment assistance;
$1 billion for farmworker, tribal, and student housing;
$500 million for housing infrastructure; and
$200 million to support local housing programs.

Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.

Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families.
The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans.
(This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst's Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable.
...
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state's housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt.
The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incur

CALIFORNIA DECIDES | Proposition Lab
PROP 1: The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
Download PDF (https://hoover-s3-website.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/s3fs-public/2026-10/California%20Decides_Proposition%201.pdf)
Research
Quick Facts
Key Questions
Risks & Benefits
California Decides (https://cms.hoover.org/publications/california-decides)
Quick Facts
Official ballot title: The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026 (SB 417, Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026, Limón).
Type: Legislative referral (general obligation bond act). Placed by the legislature, not by citizen signatures.
A vote YES means: The state may borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds. This includes about $10 billion in general obligation bonds that would fund affordable housing construction, rehabilitation, and homeownership programs, repaid from the general fund, and about $1.25 billion in revenue bonds funding CalVet home loans, repaid by the veterans who borrow.
A vote NO means: The state does not authorize this borrowing. Existing state housing programs continue with whatever money remains from prior bonds and the annual budget.
Sponsor/proponent: Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón (lead Senate author) and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas (lead Assembly author), with Gov. Gavin Newsom, who signed the measure onto the ballot June 25, 2026.
On the ballot because: The legislature passed SB 417 by the required two-thirds vote and the governor signed it. Bond acts must go to the voters. The Senate concurred twenty-nine to two on June 25, 2026.
Full legal text: SB 417, California Legislative Information (leginfo) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417)
LAO analysis: Legislative Analyst’s Office ballot analysis, Proposition 1 (2026) (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2026)
1. What would it do?
Proposition 1 asks California voters for permission to borrow $11.25 billion by selling bonds, with the money directed at affordable housing and veteran homeownership. It is a general obligation bond measure, which is the standard way the state borrows for long-lived investments and pays the money back over time out of the annual budget—requiring higher tax revenues or lower spending on other items.
The measure splits into two very different pieces. The larger piece is $10 billion in general obligation bonds for what it calls affordable housing programs (and what detractors call “subsidized” housing programs). That money would refill the state’s main housing accounts, most of which have spent down the funds from the last housing bond, 2018’s Proposition 1. The bill directs $5.1 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program that finances rental construction, with another $1.15 billion inside that program reserved for housing tied to homelessness and social programs aimed at homelessness. Smaller amounts go to homeownership help, farmworker housing, tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure that supports new residential building.
The smaller piece is $1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program, which offers below-market mortgages to veterans. This piece matters for how voters should read the price tag. CalVet loans are mostly repaid by the veterans who take them out, so this portion is designed to carry its own cost rather than fall on the general fund. The headline number is $11.25 billion, but the part that taxpayers repay is the $10 billion housing bond.
2. The legal language
Full text: SB 417, “The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act of 2026,” California Legislative Information (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) (Chapter 16, Statutes of 2026)
Key language:
“Bonds in the total amount of ten billion dollars ($10,000,000,000), exclusive of refunding bonds issued pursuant to Section 54076, or so much thereof as is necessary as determined by the committee, are hereby authorized to be issued and sold.”
What it amends: Adds Part 16.1 (commencing with Section 54050) to Division 31 of the Health and Safety Code, which houses the affordable housing programs, and Article 5ab (commencing with Section 998.750) to the Military and Veterans Code, which authorizes the CalVet loan bonds. Because a bond act is enacted by the voters, the legislature cannot repeal it on its own, though it does set the program rules that govern how the money is spent.
3. What, Where, When, Why?
Who authored it? Authored by Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón and Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, backed by Governor Newsom and a large roster of Democratic coauthors, along with a coalition of housing developers, labor, and veterans’ groups who would receive the subsidies. The named opposition is a small number of Republican legislators and free-market groups such as the Pacific Research Institute.The bond passed with almost no Republican support, and the Senate concurrence vote was twenty-nine to two.
What does it do? Authorization to sell $11.25 billion in bonds: roughly $10 billion in general obligation bonds for affordable rental housing, homeownership assistance, farmworker and tribal housing, student housing, and infrastructure, plus $1.25 billion in revenue bonds for CalVet home loans.
Where does it apply? Statewide. The money flows through existing state housing programs administered chiefly by the Department of Housing and Community Development and the Department of Veterans Affairs.
When would it take effect? Decided on the November 3, 2026, ballot. If approved, the state would sell the bonds over several years as projects come online and repay them over roughly twenty-five years.
Why did supporters put it on the ballot? Supporters point to California’s housing affordability and homelessness crisis and argue the state needs a dedicated capital source because prior bond money is nearly gone. Their stated goals are to build and preserve “affordable” homes, expand homeownership for lower-income residents and veterans, and leverage federal and private dollars.
4. Trade-offs
A bond is first and last a borrowing and subsequent repayment decision. The Legislative Analyst estimates that repaying the $10 billion housing portion would cost the general fund roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years. That is money committed to interest and principal for a quarter century, unavailable for schools, healthcare, or anything else, and locked in regardless of the state’s budget condition in any given year. California’s independent analyst frames the real cost plainly. Paying for these programs with borrowed money rather than cash on hand costs the state about 15 percent more after adjusting for inflation. In nominal dollars the gap is larger. One outside estimate puts total repayment near $17.4 billion, of which about $7.4 billion is interest, so a large share of every repayment dollar buys interest rather than housing. Either way, the honest statement is that borrowing is not free, and the premium is the price of building now instead of later.
The case for paying that premium is not weak, and voters should weigh it fairly. Housing is a long-lived asset, and financing long-lived assets with long-term debt is a defensible match, the same logic a family uses for a mortgage. The programs the bond refills are largely spent out, so the practical alternative is not cheaper cash, it is less housing built during a severe shortage. Supporters also argue that each state dollar pulls in roughly four dollars of federal tax credits, local funds, and private capital, which means the state’s borrowing is not the whole capital stack but a match that unlocks the rest.
Voters should also consider the usefulness of government-provided and allocated so-called affordable housing. The record of massive cost overruns (hundreds of thousands of dollars for tiny homeless units) is not encouraging. Affordable housing is really taxpayer-subsidized housing. When it is allocated to people with low incomes, people have to win lotteries and then face the danger of losing their housing subsidies if they earn more money or have an opportunity to get a better job if they move. It can lock people into poverty. The state and cities already pour large amounts into so-called affordable housing directly, and this plan would force developers to create such housing in return for permission to build market-rate housing. Voters should consider if more is needed. Finally, the central source of the housing affordability crisis is the state’s and cities’ limitations on private housing construction. Creating more government-subsidized and politically allocated housing instead of simply allowing people to build houses would, arguably, only make the crisis worse.
That is the trade-off. On one side, a $500 million to $600 million annual claim on the budget for twenty-five years and an inflation-adjusted premium of about 15 percent for borrowing rather than paying cash. On the other side, potentially tens of thousands of affordable and supportive homes financed during a housing emergency, with outside money leveraged on top, but potentially more boondoggles. This bond does nothing to cut the existing red tape around building “affordable” housing. The sharper question is not whether housing is worth building. It is whether a general obligation bond, repaid by all taxpayers over a generation, to fund government provision and allocation of more housing, is the right tool, or whether the same goal should compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against everything else each year.
5. Potential risks and benefits
Potential benefits
Refills the state’s main affordable housing accounts, most of which have drained the 2018 bond funds, so the money would sustain construction during a severe shortage.
Directs the largest share, $5.1 billion, to the Multifamily Housing Program, with $1.15 billion for supportive housing aimed at homelessness.
Matches long-term debt to a long-lived asset, the same financing logic used for other capital investments.
Reportedly leverages roughly four dollars of federal, local, and private capital for each state dollar, expanding the total built.
Expands homeownership at little direct taxpayer cost since the $1.25 billion CalVet portion is designed to be repaid by veteran borrowers, not the general fund.
Potential risks
Commits the general fund to roughly $500 million to $600 million a year for about twenty-five years, money unavailable for other priorities regardless of the state’s fiscal condition.
Produces borrowing costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying for the same programs with cash, and a large share of nominal repayment is interest.
Arrives as California faces budget deficits, adding a fixed cost on top of existing bond debt already near $6 billion a year in debt service.
Says nothing about the permitting, land, and labor costs that drive California’s high per-unit building costs, so more money does not guarantee proportionally more units.
Accepts that the leverage and unit-count claims come largely from proponents and assumes federal credits and local matches materialize as projected.
Builds housing that by definition does not pay for itself, leading people to live where they do not want to live and trapping them away from economic opportunity. There’s a potential for great waste.
6. Open questions
What will each subsidized unit actually cost to build with this money, and how many homes will $10 billion buy at current California construction costs?
Who will get them and how?
Does bond financing add enough housing sooner to justify the inflation-adjusted premium over paying cash through the budget?
How firm is the “four dollars leveraged per state dollar” claim once federal credit availability and local matches are tested?
Given projected deficits, what other spending gives way when $500 million to $600 million a year is committed to debt service for twenty-five years?
How much of the money reaches new construction versus preservation and program overhead, and who tracks the units delivered?
7. The questions to ask before you vote
A bond is a decision to build now and pay later, with interest. The Legislative Analyst’s Office says borrowing for these housing programs costs about 15 percent more after inflation than paying cash. Before you vote, ask whether building affordable homes during this shortage is worth that premium and a $500 million to $600 million yearly claim on the budget for the next twenty-five years.
Almost every voter wants more affordable housing. But government-provided housing is not more affordable to the state as a whole. It is only affordable to the select few recipients because taxpayers pay for it. The real question is the tool. Should this spending be locked in as bond debt that all taxpayers repay over a generation, or should it compete for cash in the annual budget where it can be weighed against schools, healthcare, and everything else each year?

Here’s what $44 billion would buy by Mikhail Zinshteyn (https://calmatters.org/author/mikhailzinshteyn/) October 24, 2026 Updated October 25, 2026 Republish Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Share on WhatsApp (Opens in new window) WhatsApp (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/bond-measures-on-california-ballot/) Construction in a residential area that was burned during the Eaton Fire in 2025, in Altadena, on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Jules Hotz for CalMatters In summary Californians will decide on $44 billion in bonds when the vote on Propositions 1, 37 and 38. They’d take out debt to pay for housing and medical research. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. Your November ballot is welcoming you to make it rain … in bonds. You’ll see an El Nino-sized set of propositions that could flood the housing construction and science research components of the California economy with $44 billion of bond spending if the measures pass. Two of those bond proposals — Proposition 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/) for housing and Proposition 38 (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) for immunology research — are the traditional borrow-now, pay-back-later arrangements that add a few billion dollars to the overall cost of the propositions. A third, Proposition 37 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/), is an atypical measure that amounts to a low-risk radical experiment that taxpayers likely won’t be on the hook for, at least not directly. Historically, bond propositions win the approval of voters at higher rates than other measures. Since 2000, voters passed 23 of the 26 statewide bonds before them, an 88% yay rate. In recent years voters approved billions in bond debt for school construction, combatting the effects of climate change and housing for veterans. Bonds are a form of debt that the state must pay off over time, and that means annual payments with interest (https://voterguide.sos.ca.gov/voter-info/overview-state-bond-debt.htm). The state spends $6 billion annually to repay about $80 billion of bonds. Voters and lawmakers have also approved $40 billion in bonds that have yet to be sold. Fortunately for your ballot studying, the following cheat sheet is a primer on just the three bonds before you. Prop. 1: Affordable housing If voters say yes, Prop. 1 would permit California’s treasurer (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-1-housing-bond/) to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds. That money would provide various types of housing, including to veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes. The measure dedicates $7 billion to constructing, refurbishing, or acquiring apartment complexes, primarily through loans to developers of affordable housing. These developments must serve low-income residents, reserving at least 10% of units for extremely low-income households. Over $1 billion of this total supports permanent and interim housing for the homeless. The bond, if passed, would result in some 40,000 new rental units, wrote (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) the Legislative Analyst’s Office, which is the nonpartisan think-tank of the Legislature. This is the only bond measure on the ballot put forward by lawmakers. The other two secured enough signatures from voters to secure a spot for the November election. Opposition to this bond is minimal. The state Republican Party’s officially neutral on the measure. Several Republican lawmakers in June voted no on the bill that metamorphosed into this bond. They argued that the bill’s title — The Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act (https://calmatters.digitaldemocracy.org/bills/ca_202520260sb417) — misled the public on just how much of the bond revenue would support veterans. The answer? $1.25 billion for veterans to secure home loans. Another $350 million would head to the state’s two public university systems to help finance the development of student dorms. But with costs per bed often exceeding $250,000, all those tens of millions of dollars would secure dorms for around 1,300 students. Get California’s most essential headlines without feeling overwhelmed. Email address By clicking subscribe, you agree to the terms (https://calmatters.org/about/policies-and-standards/). Sign up for free Δ Support for Prop. 1 is vast, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, the state Democratic party, home-sharing company AirBnB, major unions and more. Want more? Read CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall’s guide to Prop. 1 (https://calmatters.org/housing/homelessness/2026/10/prop-1-housing-bond/). Prop. 37: Help for down payments This bond measure is strange (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-37-homebuyers-loan/), novel and introduces a bevy of unknowns. Confused? So is everyone else, which is why CalMatters’ housing reporter Ben Christopher described this unorthodox proposition as “plainly weird.” (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/prop-37-explained-homeownership/) Prop. 37 should be viewed as a way to help buyers of new homes secure down payments. The language permits individuals to apply for as much as 17% of the purchase price of a new house, condo or townhome. That covers much of the typical 20% down payment. Who’s eligible? Roughly 90% of all California renters. The income caps vary by county, so around $115,000 in Imperial and north of $400,000 in San Mateo for a family of three. Eligible homes must satisfy several conditions: They’re new or newly converted and don’t cost more than roughly $1.5 million in the Bay Area or $1 million in Riverside — again, it’s based on a weedy formula by county. What won’t it do? Add to the state’s debt repayment log. This is not a bond that taxpayers will pay back; instead private lenders who provide this bond money will be repaid by homebuyers in the form of interest payments. How many homes this could buy is impossible to predict. That number depends on how much the new homes cost, the incomes of the homebuyers and whether developers build new homes. Most renters today couldn’t afford even the cheapest new homes, said Eric McGhee, an analyst for the nonprofit Public Policy Institute of California who’s written about Prop. 37 (https://www.ppic.org/blog/how-many-might-actually-use-the-down-payment-assistance-in-proposition-37/). He estimated that anywhere from 60,000 to more than 1.8 million buyers could take advantage of the down payment assistance through this bond measure. The lower end assumes a 20% down payment on the most expensive homes. The higher end assumes 5% down payments on the least expensive homes. Prop. 38: Immunology research This bond proposal (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-38-research-bond/) would commit $4.2 billion to a single, unnamed nonprofit institute that focuses on immunology research and cures for major diseases such as Alzheimer’s, cancer and heart disease. The same amount would be distributed to a committee that’d identify a limited number of researchers at public universities and nonprofits who study immunology and immunotherapies. Previous reporting by CalMatters (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/07/proposition-38-california/) found only one institute in California currently meets Prop. 38’s criteria for half of the money: the California Institute for Immunology and Immunotherapy. The institute’s primary funder is billionaire Gary K. Michelson, who wrote Prop. 38 and is by far the largest donor to its political campaign. Additional CalMatters reporting raises the question of how ready is the institute to implement the bond’s vast dollars. The institute had only three employees (https://calmatters.org/politics/elections/2026/10/prop-38-california/) as of last month, far fewer than the 51 it planned to have on staff last year. The Yes on 38 campaign says the bond revenue is needed to hedge against the Trump administration’s ongoing efforts to cut federal science research or limit what’s studied. They argue that any curtailment of drug trials and other therapies can lead to avoidable pain and death for patients of debilitating maladies. Opponents of the measure fault it for concentrating half the money in a single institute and limiting which other researchers can receive the funding. They say science research is best performed in a competitive environment that’s open to all of California’s nonprofit and public university scientists.
